title: Making Music

image.credit: Private collection (as stated on source page); via arthistoryproject.com

altText: A small oil painting on panel with cats as its subject, titled Making Music. The title suggests the cats are part of a musical scene.

source.museum: Private collection (as stated on source page)
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, collection, public-domain statement)

context: An oil painting on panel by Henriëtte Ronner-Knip, dated 1900 (the source page gives c.1900). The source page says it is in a private collection and tags it Cats. The title tells us it is about making music.

descriptions.k: This painting is called Making Music. Look for the cats in the picture. What do you think they are doing? Can you pretend to make the same sound?
descriptions.g12: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip painted Making Music around 1900. The painting has cats in it, and the title tells us it is about music. Look closely at the cats. What do you think they are doing? What sound would you hear if you could step inside the picture?
descriptions.g35: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip made this small oil painting on a wooden panel around 1900. The source page tags it with cats, and the title is Making Music. A painter of animals has to watch very carefully. Look at the cats' fur, ears and eyes. What details show that the painter studied real cats?
descriptions.g68: Ronner-Knip's Making Music (about 1900) is an oil painting on panel tagged with cats, and the playful title invites you to imagine a musical moment among animals. Painters of pets in this period often gave animals human activities to charm viewers. How might the title change the way you read the cats' poses and expressions? Point to evidence you can see.
descriptions.g910: Making Music (about 1900) is an oil on panel by Ronner-Knip, whose work is known for its attention to cats. The title sets up a gentle humor by linking animals with a human pastime. Consider how the painter balances close observation of the animals with a staged, story-like idea. Which details feel observed from life, and which feel arranged for effect?
descriptions.g1112: Ronner-Knip's Making Music (c.1900) joins careful animal observation to an anthropomorphic premise suggested by its title, a strategy common in popular domestic painting of the period. Such pictures were made for private homes, and this one remains in a private collection. How does the work balance sincerity and humor, and what does it suggest about how people of the time wanted to see their pets? Weigh visual evidence against the limits of what the title alone tells us.

k.daily: Look for the cats. How many cats can you find?
k.emotion: How does this picture make you feel? Happy, calm or sleepy?
k.observation: Point to something soft in the painting. What is it?
k.analysis: Which cat do you look at first? What made you look there?
k.line: Trace the outline of one cat in the air with your finger. Is it curvy or straight?
k.shape: Find a round shape in the painting. What is it part of?
k.color: Point to the brightest color you can find. What is it on?
k.texture: Imagine petting a cat in this picture. How would its fur feel?
k.space: Which cat looks closest to you? Which looks farthest away?
k.light: Where is the lightest spot in the painting?
k.meaning: The painting is called Making Music. What sound do you think you would hear?
k.culture: People have kept cats as pets for a very long time. How do you take care of a pet, or how would you?
k.technique: The painter used a thin wooden board instead of cloth. Can you find where the paint looks smooth?
k.personal: If you could be a cat in this painting, what would you do?
k.critical: What would you name this painting if it did not have a title?

g12.daily: What do you think the title Making Music is telling us about the cats?
g12.emotion: What feeling do you get from this painting, and which part gives you that feeling?
g12.observation: Name three things you can find in the painting besides the cats.
g12.analysis: Which cat is the main one? How can you tell?
g12.line: How did the painter make the lines of the fur look soft and fuzzy?
g12.shape: What shapes make up the body of a cat, such as circles for the head?
g12.color: Which colors are used most for the cats? Which colors are used for the background?
g12.texture: How did the painter show that the cats' fur is soft and not hard?
g12.space: What helps you tell which cat is in front and which is behind?
g12.light: Where does the light fall on the cats, and where is it darker?
g12.meaning: What story could you tell about what happens right before and after this picture?
g12.culture: Many families in 1900 kept cats at home. What might people have liked about a painting of cats?
g12.technique: The painter used oil paint on a flat wooden panel. What small details can you see that needed tiny brushes?
g12.personal: What music would you play to go with this painting?
g12.critical: What would change in the picture if the cats were not there?

g35.daily: What small details of the cats, such as whiskers, ears or paws, show careful looking?
g35.emotion: What mood does the painting set, and which details support your idea?
g35.observation: Describe one cat from head to tail using words for color, shape and texture.
g35.analysis: How are the cats arranged, and what does that arrangement make you look at first?
g35.line: How do the painted lines and brushstrokes follow the direction of the fur?
g35.shape: Which curved shapes do you find in the cats' bodies, and how do they connect to each other?
g35.color: How do the colors of the fur stand out from, or blend into, the background?
g35.texture: What painting techniques could make fur look soft and whiskers look thin?
g35.space: How does the painter use overlap to show which cats are nearer to us?
g35.light: How does light on the fur help the cats look rounded and real?
g35.meaning: The title is Making Music. How does knowing it change what you think the cats are doing?
g35.culture: Painters in the 1800s often made pictures people could hang in their homes. Why might a cat painting be a popular choice?
g35.technique: This is a small painting on a wooden panel. How might a small size help a painter include fine detail?
g35.personal: What would you want to know about the cats if you could ask the painter?
g35.critical: How is a painting of cats different from a photograph of cats?

g68.daily: What clues in the image suggest the cats are involved in something deliberate rather than just posing?
g68.emotion: How do the cats' postures and expressions shape the emotional tone of the work?
g68.observation: Compare how the painter handles the cats with how she handles their surroundings. What do you notice?
g68.analysis: How does the placement of the cats organize the composition and guide your eye?
g68.line: How do the direction and length of brushstrokes help describe fur and movement?
g68.shape: How do the overall shapes of the cats' bodies create a rhythm across the panel?
g68.color: How does the color range of the fur interact with the setting to create harmony or contrast?
g68.texture: What would a painter need to do with oil paint to make fur seem soft, soft-edged and detailed at once?
g68.space: How does the painter create depth in a fairly small painting?
g68.light: How does the direction of light shape the cats' forms and mood?
g68.meaning: How does the idea of making music turn an ordinary pet scene into a story?
g68.culture: Why might paintings that gave pets human-like activities appeal to people around 1900?
g68.technique: What choices of detail and blurring suggest that the painter studied living cats?
g68.personal: If you were to stage your own scene of animals doing something human, which activity would you choose and why?
g68.critical: Why might a mostly charming painting still deserve serious attention? Use details from the work to argue.

g910.daily: Which details feel closely observed, and which feel invented to fit the title Making Music?
g910.emotion: How does the painting balance gentle humor with sincere affection for its subjects?
g910.observation: Examine the rendering of fur, eyes and whiskers. What do they reveal about Ronner-Knip's technical priorities?
g910.analysis: How does the composition build a focal point, and what secondary elements support it?
g910.line: How do directional strokes and contours create a sense of movement in otherwise still animals?
g910.shape: How do the rounded masses of the cats contrast with other forms in the scene?
g910.color: How does the palette contribute to the sense of warmth or intimacy, and what evidence supports your reading?
g910.texture: How does the treatment of surface differentiate animal fur from the other materials in the picture?
g910.space: How does the arrangement of figures within the panel's limited format create a sense of depth or enclosure?
g910.light: How does the handling of light and shadow add volume and a sense of atmosphere to the animals?
g910.meaning: What does the pairing of cats with a human pastime suggest about how pets were imagined in the period?
g910.culture: How might a painting like this reflect nineteenth-century attitudes toward domestic life and leisure?
g910.technique: How does Ronner-Knip's choice of oil on panel suit a highly finished, detailed treatment?
g910.personal: What does this painting make you consider about how people project their own activities onto animals?
g910.critical: To what extent does the title direct our interpretation, and how would the image read without it?

g1112.daily: How does the painting use the premise of musical activity to frame animal behavior as a quasi-human narrative?
g1112.emotion: In what ways might the tone shift between tenderness and gentle satire, depending on how closely you read the animals?
g1112.observation: Scrutinize the passages where fur, eyes and edges are resolved. What do they reveal about the painter's pursuit of illusion?
g1112.analysis: How do compositional choices organize a hierarchy among the figures and direct narrative attention?
g1112.line: How does the rhythm of contour and stroke suggest motion in what is, strictly, a frozen moment?
g1112.shape: How do mass and silhouette function in the picture, and what do they suggest about the stability of the scene?
g1112.color: How might the chromatic choices reinforce a domestic, comfortable sensibility, and how would you test that against the image?
g1112.texture: How does the surface finish connect to the market for polished cabinet-sized pictures in this period?
g1112.space: How does the painter use the compressed space of a small panel to produce intimacy without sacrificing legibility?
g1112.light: How does the modelling of form through light support the credibility of an arranged scene?
g1112.meaning: How does anthropomorphism in popular painting both flatter viewers and reveal the assumptions behind the way they saw animals?
g1112.culture: Given that the work remains in a private collection, how does its likely history of ownership shape what we can responsibly claim about its reception?
g1112.technique: How does the technique of oil on panel enable effects that would be difficult on canvas, and where might you see them here?
g1112.personal: How do your own experiences of living with or observing animals influence the way you interpret the work?
g1112.critical: What is the strongest argument that a charming genre painting like this deserves critical attention, and what evidence in the image would support it?

teacherNote.context: An oil painting on panel by Henriëtte Ronner-Knip, dated around 1900, in a private collection. The source page tags it Cats; the title is Making Music. The page gives no further description, so check the image with students before discussing what the cats are doing.
directions: Ask students to look for ten details of the cats before they say what they think the painting shows.
Invite younger students to draw their own pet or an animal making music, using soft strokes for fur.
Ask older students to discuss why artists give animals human activities and how a title guides what we see.
